subject: psychology
title: Aggression & Violence: Foundations
welcome_lead: Start with biological explanations of aggression.
meta_desc: GCSE Psychology adventure on biological aggression: testosterone, amygdala and the limbic system.
final_note: You can explain biological roots of aggression.

walkthroughs.body_html: Higher testosterone levels correlate with increased aggression in many studies. Prison studies show inmates with violent crimes often have higher testosterone. However, correlation does not prove causation — context matters.

The amygdala triggers anger and fear responses. Studies of brain-damaged patients show changes in aggression. The limbic system also includes the hippocampus and hypothalamus, which regulate emotional responses.

Low serotonin levels are linked to impulsive aggression. Serotonin usually inhibits the firing of neurons in the prefrontal cortex; without enough, impulses are harder to control. SSRIs sometimes reduce aggressive outbursts.
